title: Being a Public School Kid
author: Brian Auten
summary: The author, a self-described "public school kid," uses the biography of his own kindergarten teacher to push back on the conservative Christian narrative that public schools function as "leftist indoctrination factories." His 1974 kindergarten teacher, Mrs. Mary Higuchi, taught her Torrance, California class basic Japanese language and culture; the essay reveals that she had been interned as a young child at the Poston War Relocation Center during World War II, and traces her family's post-internment life, her mother's insistence on education despite hardship, and Mrs. Higuchi's later career as an artist reckoning with that history through her "EO 9066" painting series. The piece pivots into a critique of current evangelical debates that dismiss empathy as manipulative or "toxic," arguing that Mrs. Higuchi's classroom modeled something different: a "classically humanist" teaching of love, connection, and honoring a neighboring community's culture on its own terms, without ideological framing or appeals to pity. The author frames this as an example of what public education can do at its best, and as something he believes is in short supply today.
points: The author uses his own kindergarten teacher's biography — a Japanese-American internment survivor who taught Japanese language and culture in a 1970s Torrance public school — to push back on the conservative Christian narrative that public schools are "indoctrination factories."

Mrs. Higuchi's family was interned at Poston for three years during WWII; her later art (the "EO 9066" series) reconstructed that history through mixed media, drawing on her mother's rarely-shared memories.

The essay argues her classroom approach wasn't "toxic empathy" or ideological instruction, but something more "classically humanist" — teaching children to love and honor a neighboring community's language and culture on its own terms.

It frames the piece as a rebuttal to current evangelical debates that dismiss empathy as manipulative, arguing that acknowledging painful history to children can be done through love and connection rather than pity or political messaging.
quotes: Since the 1960s, conservative Christians have railed against public schools as little more than "leftist indoctrination factories.

When she was just three years old, on 6 August 1942, Hatsuko Yoshioka, her parents, Goro and Kiyoko Yoshioka, and her younger sister, Etsuko, were removed from their South Bay home and arrived at the Poston War Relocation Center.
In each of the housing barracks, four families were typically allotted 500 square feet of living space each.
Her parents saved enough money to purchase their own property, but, in November 1951, right before they could move, Goro Yoshioka, who had been ill on-and-off at Poston, died of heart failure.

This war on empathy has done little but produce a greater coarsening among fellow Christians in the public square, particularly when one talks about the more distasteful, horrible moments of American history.
There was nothing remotely directly or indirectly "woke" or "leftist" about Mrs. Higuchi's public school classroom. There was no "indoctrination.
She taught love. She taught us to love Japanese language, to love Japanese culture, and to love Japanese Americans, and to love them all together with one another.
